summary.text: Counting primes through residue classes coprime to moduli $30030$ (with a subsidiary estimate modulo $210$) yields the explicit bound $\pi(5X)\le X$ for $X\ge175000$, so induction bounds every term by $175000$ plus the sum of the five initial values. Consequently only finitely many consecutive five-term states can occur; two states repeat by the pigeonhole principle, and the deterministic recurrence propagates that equality forever, giving eventual periodicity.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\pi(x)\) denote the number of primes less than or equal to \(x\). For a choice of five initial values
\[
v=(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4)\in \mathbb N^5,
\]
define \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
a_j=v_j\quad(0\le j<5)
\]
and
\[
a_{i+5}=\pi(a_i+a_{i+1}+a_{i+2}+a_{i+3}+a_{i+4})
\quad(i\ge0).
\]
We prove that this sequence is ultimately periodic. In fact, the argument works even if some of the initial values are zero, so the assumed positivity is more than is needed.

We first establish a numerical estimate for the prime-counting function.

Write \(\pi_{<}(y)\) for the number of primes strictly less than \(y\), so that
\[
\pi(x)=\pi_{<}(x+1).
\]
We use the following elementary counting inequality. If \(m\ne0\), \(m<k\), and \(t\ge0\), then
\[
\pi_{<}(k+t)
 \le \pi_{<}(k)+\varphi(m)\left(\left\lfloor\frac{t}{m}\right\rfloor+1\right), \tag{1}
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function.

Indeed, split the primes below \(k+t\) into those below \(k\) and those in the interval \([k,k+t)\). Every prime \(p\) in the latter interval satisfies \(p\ge k>m\). Consequently \(p\) cannot divide \(m\), and since \(p\) is prime this implies \(\gcd(p,m)=1\). In any block of \(m\) consecutive integers, exactly \(\varphi(m)\) integers are coprime to \(m\), because the block contains each residue class modulo \(m\) exactly once. The interval \([k,k+t)\) can be covered by \(\lfloor t/m\rfloor+1\) such blocks (the last block may only be partially used). Thus the number of possible primes in that interval is at most the second term on the right side of (1), proving the inequality.

We shall apply (1) with the moduli \(210\) and \(30030\). Their totients are
\[
\varphi(210)=48,
\qquad
\varphi(30030)=5760. \tag{2}
\]
For completeness, the second value may be computed by the factorization
\[
30030=10\cdot3003,
\qquad 3003=21\cdot143.
\]
The factors in each displayed product are coprime, so multiplicativity of the totient gives
\[
\varphi(30030)=\varphi(10)\varphi(21)\varphi(143)
=4\cdot12\cdot120=5760.
\]
Here \(143=11\cdot13\), whence \(\varphi(143)=(11-1)(13-1)=120\). Likewise, from \(210=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\),
\[
\varphi(210)=210\left(1-\frac12\right)
\left(1-\frac13\right)
\left(1-\frac15\right)
\left(1-\frac17\right)=48.
\]

First use (1) with
\[
m=210,\qquad k=211,\qquad t=29820.
\]
Since \(211+29820=30031\), and since trivially \(\pi_{<}(211)\le211\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{<}(30031)
&\le \pi_{<}(211)+48\left(\left\lfloor\frac{29820}{210}\right\rfloor+1\right)\\
&\le211+48(142+1)\\
&=7075. \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
This estimate is deliberately crude, but it is sufficient.

We now prove that
\[
\pi(5X)\le X\qquad\text{for every }X\ge175000. \tag{4}
\]
Fix such an \(X\). Apply (1) with
\[
m=30030,\qquad k=30031,
\qquad t=5X-30030.
\]
The assumption on \(X\) ensures that \(t\) is a nonnegative integer, and
\[
k+t=30031+(5X-30030)=5X+1.
\]
Using (2) and (3), and observing that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{5X-30030}{30030}\right\rfloor+1
=
\left\lfloor\frac{5X}{30030}\right\rfloor,
\]
we get
\[
\pi(5X)=\pi_{<}(5X+1)
\le7075+5760\left\lfloor\frac{5X}{30030}\right\rfloor. \tag{5}
\]
Set
\[
q=\left\lfloor\frac{5X}{30030}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because \(X\ge175000\),
\[
5X\ge875000\ge870870=29\cdot30030,
\]
so \(q\ge29\). On the other hand, by the defining property of the floor,
\[
30030q\le5X.
\]
As \(30030=5\cdot6006\), cancellation of the positive factor \(5\) gives
\[
6006q\le X. \tag{6}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
6006q-5760q=246q\ge246\cdot29=7134\ge7075.
\]
Therefore
\[
7075+5760q\le6006q\le X.
\]
Combining this with (5) proves (4).

We next use (4) to show that every term of the recurrence is bounded. Define
\[
B=175000+v_0+v_1+v_2+v_3+v_4. \tag{7}
\]
We claim that
\[
a_n\le B\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0. \tag{8}
\]
We prove this by strong induction on \(n\).

For \(0\le n<5\), we have \(a_n=v_n\), and clearly \(v_n\le B\) by (7). Now let \(n=i+5\), and suppose that (8) holds for every index below \(n\). In particular,
\[
a_i,a_{i+1},a_{i+2},a_{i+3},a_{i+4}\le B.
\]
Hence
\[
a_i+a_{i+1}+a_{i+2}+a_{i+3}+a_{i+4}\le5B.
\]
The prime-counting function is nondecreasing, so the recurrence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i+5}
&=\pi(a_i+a_{i+1}+a_{i+2}+a_{i+3}+a_{i+4})\\
&\le\pi(5B).
\end{aligned}
\]
By definition, \(B\ge175000\), and thus (4), applied with \(X=B\), yields
\[
\pi(5B)\le B.
\]
Therefore \(a_{i+5}\le B\), completing the induction and proving (8).

Now consider, for every \(n\ge0\), the state consisting of five consecutive terms:
\[
S_n=(a_n,a_{n+1},a_{n+2},a_{n+3},a_{n+4}). \tag{9}
\]
By (8), each coordinate of every \(S_n\) belongs to the finite set
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,B\}.
\]
Thus there are at most \((B+1)^5\) possible states. Since the infinite list
\[
S_0,S_1,S_2,\ldots
\]
takes values in this finite set, two of its entries must be equal. Hence there exist integers \(N<b\) such that
\[
S_N=S_b. \tag{10}
\]
Let
\[
P=b-N.
\]
Then \(P>0\), \(b=N+P\), and equality (10) says precisely that
\[
a_{N+P+j}=a_{N+j}
\qquad(0\le j<5). \tag{11}
\]

It remains to show that equality of these two five-term states forces equality forever. We prove by strong induction on \(r\ge0\) that
\[
a_{N+P+r}=a_{N+r}. \tag{12}
\]
For \(r=0,1,2,3,4\), this is exactly (11). Suppose now that \(r\ge5\), write \(r=i+5\), and assume (12) for every smaller nonnegative integer. The five integers \(i,i+1,i+2,i+3,i+4\) are all less than \(i+5=r\), so the induction hypothesis gives
\[
a_{N+P+i+j}=a_{N+i+j}
\qquad(0\le j<5). \tag{13}
\]
Both terms in (12) at index \(r=i+5\) are governed by the recurrence, because they occur at indices at least \(5\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{N+P+i+5}
&=\pi\bigl(a_{N+P+i}+a_{N+P+i+1}+a_{N+P+i+2}
+a_{N+P+i+3}+a_{N+P+i+4}\bigr),\\
a_{N+i+5}
&=\pi\bigl(a_{N+i}+a_{N+i+1}+a_{N+i+2}
+a_{N+i+3}+a_{N+i+4}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The five summands in the first line equal the corresponding five summands in the second line by (13). The sums, and hence their prime counts, are equal. This proves (12) for \(r\), completing the strong induction.

Finally, let \(n\ge N\). Write \(n=N+r\), where \(r=n-N\ge0\). Equation (12) gives
\[
a_{n+P}=a_{N+r+P}=a_{N+P+r}=a_{N+r}=a_n.
\]
Thus there exist \(N\in\mathbb N\) and a positive period \(P\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
a_{n+P}=a_n\qquad\text{for every }n\ge N.
\]
Hence the sequence arising from every choice of five positive initial values is ultimately periodic.
